Viṣṇudharmottarapurāṇa
------------------------------------------
Though classed among the upa-पुराणस्, this is an important work quite extensive and encyclopaedic in nature. It is in three sections. The following is a very brief account of its contents; geography, अस्त्रोनोम्य् and अस्त्रोलोग्य्; pacification of unfavourable स्तर्स् and plants; omens and portents; मर्रिअगे and duties of women; penances; vratas or religious vows and observances; śrāddhas (funeral rites); duties of Vaiṣṇavas; science of war and allied topics; medical sciences; मुसिच् and dancing; sculpture and Vaiṣṇava theology.
It might have been compiled around A.

to 500.
Its contents have been widely used by the writers of धर्मशास्त्रस्.

Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta Darśana
------------------------------------------
Introduction
Among the well-known philosophical systems of India, the Vedānta system—called the ‘Vedānta दर्शन’ and based mainly on the प्रस्थानत्रय viz., the उपनिषद्स्, the Brahmasūtras and the Bhagavadgītā—has carved out for itself a pre-eminent place. This system has, in course of time, branched off into three main streams: Advaita, Viśiṣṭādvaita and द्वैत.
The विशिष्टाद्वैत वेदान्त दर्शन, is not the च्रेअतिओन् of Rāmānuja (A.
-1137) as many believe, but much older than him. The twelve आऌवार्स् like नम्माऌवार्, Kulaśekhara and आण्डाऌ (A.
-900), as also the Ācāryas like नाथमुनि (A.
-924), Yāmuna (A.

-1038) and Rāmānuja evolved the system out of the more ancient teachings contained in the प्रस्थानत्रय and gave it a definite shape. However, Rāmānuja was its best exponent. The pioneering and stupendous work he has turned out in the cause of this system, perhaps, justifies in its being sometimes called ‘Rāmānuja दर्शन’.
The demise of Rāmānuja was followed by a period of sectarian split among his followers (generally called ‘Śrīvaiṣṇavas’) which ultimately ended in a permanent division of their ranks into two sects of वडगलैस् and Teṅgalais. These words literally mean the followers of the northern and the southern schools respectively. The two sects developed separate sets of works, separate lineage of gurus or teachers and separate traditions in many matters of practical importance.
Mention should be made here, of the following apostolic successors of Rāmānuja who were responsible for establishing the system on a firm foundation: वेदान्त देशिक (A.
-1370), पिऌऌऐ लोकाचार्य (A.
-1327) and Māṇavāḷa Māmuni (A.

-1443).
Literature
The canonical works of this system are: Gītārthasaṅgraha of Yāmuna; Vedārtha-saṅgraha, Śrībhāṣya and Gītā-bhāṣya of Rāmānuja; Tātparyacandrikā, Īśāvāsyabhāṣya and Rahasyatrayasāra of वेदान्त देशिक and Śrutaprakāśikā of सुदर्शन Sūri (A.
-1275). The Tamil compositions of the आऌवार्स् (called Nālāyira-prabandham) and quite a few compositions of other teachers like Raṅga-rāmānuja (A.

) are also considered very authoritative.
Viśiṣṭādvaita is essentially a philo-sophy of religion. In it, reason and faith coalesce to become ‘reasoned faith’. It is often identified with the older ‘Seśvara Mīmāṁsā,’ and is also called ‘Ubhaya Vedānta,’ (ubhaya = both) since it accepts both the Sanskrit प्रस्थानत्रय and the Tamil prabandhams as equally authoritative. Pāñcarātra treatises are also put on a par with the वेदस्.
Epistemology
Rāmānuja accepts knowledge in all its levels of sense perception (pratyakṣa), inference (anumāna), and scriptural testimony (āgama or शब्द) as valid, and also that it affirms reality. The principle of धर्मभूतज्ञान, the logical rule of अपृथक्-सिद्ध-viśeṣaṇa, the grammatical rule of sāmānādhikaraṇya, and the realistic view of सत्कार्यवाद are the special features of his theory of knowledge.
Dharmabhūtajñāna is the चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् of the individual सोउल् as its attribute, through which it comes to know the nature of the external world, Self, and ईश्वर or ब्रह्मन्. It is eternal and all-pervasive in respect of ईश्वर and the jīvas. However, owing to the limitation imposed by कर्म, it has become contracted in the latter. When it is purified, it expands into infinity and brings about an immediate intuition of God.
The logical rule of अपृथक्-सिद्ध-viśeṣaṇa states that a viśeṣaṇa (quality) subsists in the viśeṣya (the qualified substance) and is अपृथक्-सिद्ध or has an inseparable existence. Of course, it is not absolutely identical with it. It is separate and yet inseparable. For instance, when we say that ‘man is rational,’ the quality of rationality is inseparable from man, though it is not man himself. In the view of Rāmānuja, धर्मभूतज्ञान is an अपृथक्-सिद्ध-viśeṣaṇa of the जीव; the jīvas and प्रकृति are अपृथक्-सिद्ध-viśeṣaṇa of ब्रह्मन् or ईश्वर.
This very truth is brought out by the grammatical rule of sāmānādhikaraṇya or co-ordinate predication, which means the application of two terms to a single entity through connotation of its two modes. For example, in the sentence ‘This is a cow,’ different words connoting genus and quality (i.e. जाति and गुण) also connote individual (vyakti) and substance (guṇin) respectively. Same is the case with the Upaniṣadic text ‘Tat tvam asi’ (‘That thou art’). A substance may become the body or quality of another substance, and a word connoting the body (śarīra) may connote the Self, its possessor (śarīrin) also. Therefore, in the above example, the term ‘tvam,’ which connotes the जीव as the śarīra, connotes also ब्रह्मन्, the śarīrin. Thus, in the highest Vedāntic sense, all terms connoting a thing or a person or a god connote also ब्रह्मन् as the source, support, and the ultimate Self of all.
The Sāṅkhya theory of सत्कार्यवाद, the theory of pre-existent effect, is accepted by Rāmānuja. Consequently, the world which is a transformation (pariṇāma) of ब्रह्मन्, is real and not illusory as asserted by the Advaitins.
Ontology
Viśiṣṭādvaita accepts the three entities, viz., ब्रह्मन् or ईश्वर, जीव or cit, and प्रकृति or अचित् as the ultimate realities. Hence, these three together are called ‘tattvatraya.’ Of these, however, ब्रह्मन् is the absolute, independent Reality, whereas the other two are dependent realities. It is for this reason that this philosophy is known as ‘Viśiṣṭā-द्वैत’ (Viśiṣṭa Advaita), a philosophy which accepts only one Reality, but with attributes or modes.
Brahman of Viśiṣṭādvaita is both the Absolute of philosophy and the God of religion at the same time. Truth (satya), knowledge (jñāna), infinity (anantatva), and bliss (ānandatva) are his attributes. He is the repository of all virtues and perfection. He is the progenitor, protector, and destroyer of this universe. He is also the indweller and controller of everything that exists in this universe. He is the śeṣin (the whole) of whom all the jīvas and the प्रकृति are शेष (parts). He is the granter of all boons, whether it is righteousness (dharma), worldly gain (artha), and enjoyment of pleasures (kāma) or the attainment of freedom from births and deaths (mokṣa). His form is most wonderfully beautiful, absolutely free from all imperfections and defects. Out of his infinite mercy, he incarnates himself in moments of cosmic crisis, into humanity, in order that he may recover the lost जीव. He is the master of Śrī or लक्ष्मी, Bhū, and Nīlā. Śrī is of the nature of mercy.
He enjoys the cosmic līla or play of च्रेअतिओन्. He creates this universe out of the cit and the अचित् portions of himself and yet remains unaffected in his essential nature. Since he creates in accordance with the past कर्म of the individual souls, he can never be accused of partiality or hardheartedness.
He has a five-fold form, viz., पर, vyūha, विभव, अन्तर्यामिन् and arca. The first is his form in वैकुण्ठ, along with Śrī, Bhū, Nīlā, अनन्त, गरुड, विष्वक्सेन and others. The avatāras of सङ्कर्षण, प्रद्युम्न, and अनिरुद्ध, who are his partial manifestations and who are the objects of contemplation by the devotees, go by the name ‘vyūha.’ The incarnations of राम, कृष्ण, कूर्म, etc., are called ‘vibhava’. As the indwelling spirit of each and every object (animate or inanimate), he is called the ‘antar-yāmin’. The descent into the forms, symbols, or इदोल्स् worshipped by his devotees, in order to bless them, is known as ‘arcāvatāra’.
The next tattva is cit or the जीव. The jīvas are innumerable but of identical form and nature. Each जीव is essentially different from the body, मिन्द्, प्राण, बुद्धि, and धर्मभूतज्ञान. He is blissful (ānanda-svarūpa), atomic (aṇu), unmanifested (avyakta), unthinkable (acintya), homogeneous (niravayava), immutable (nirvikāra), substratum of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् and knowledge (jñānāśraya). He is (niyamya) controlled by ईश्वर, and is a part of him (śeṣa). He is the knower of knowledge, doer of actions, and experiencer of their results (jñātṛ, kartṛ and भोक्तृ).
The jīvas can be divided into three groups: the bound (baddha), the liberated (mukta), and the eternally free (nitya). The bound souls are those who are constantly going through this transmigratory existence being attracted by and attached to the प्रकृति in all its forms. Those of the bound souls who awaken to the evils of सṁसार owing to their previous good कर्म and get liberated by doing spiritual practices and by the grace of God belong to the second category. Those like अनन्त or गरुड who are never bound by the shackles of सṁसार form the third category. The जीव, though essentially free, becomes bound in सṁसार by the proximity of प्रकृति, अविद्या, कर्म, वासना and ruci. अविद्या is इग्नोरन्चे which manifests itself in various forms like anyathā-ज्ञान (knowing a thing in a way that is different from what it really is), viparīta-ज्ञान (knowing a thing as the opposite of what it really is), etc. कर्म is what is performed by the body, the senses, or the मिन्द्, whether good or bad. Doing anything unintentionally is वासना. Ruci is the inordinate desire created by वासना. Through भक्ति and प्रपत्ति and the consequent grace of God, these bondages are destroyed.
The last tattva is अचित् or प्रकृति. It is the insentient substance out of which this material universe is evolved. It is everchanging and can never be the substratum of knowledge. It is of two kinds: शुद्धसत्त्व and miśrasattva. The first is the material which is absolutely free from रजस् and तमस्, is eternal, and is not subject to कर्म but only to the will of God. It is the substance out of which all things in वैकुण्ठ (which is called ‘nityavibhūti,’ as opposed to this temporal world, called ‘līlāvibhūti’) are made. The second, viz., miśrasattva, comprises the three guṇas—sattva, रजस् and तमस्. It is this which has evolved as this universe.
Out of these, ब्रह्मन् or ईश्वर is the independent reality, and the other two are dependent realities which inhere in him by the principle of sāmānādhikaraṇya. Just as skin, flesh, seed, colour, taste and smell can all exist in the same mango simultaneously, so also can cit and अचित् exist in ब्रह्मन्.
Means of Liberation
The mumukṣus, or those desirous of लिबेरतिओन्, have to know three things: tattva or Reality, हित or the means of attaining that Reality, and puruṣārtha or the nature of attainment. Of these, tattva has already been described.
As regards हित, the scriptures have described it in various ways. These things can be grouped under five headings, and are consequently known as ‘arthapañcaka’. They are: sva-svarūpa (one’s own nature), पर-svarūpa (nature of God), puruṣārtha-svarūpa (nature of the four ends in life), उपाय-svarūpa (nature of the means to लिबेरतिओन्), and virodhi-svarūpa (nature of the obstacles in spiritual path).
Out of these, the first two have already been delineated while describing the tattvatraya. पुरुषार्थस्, or the things desired for by men, are four in number: धर्म (practice of righteousness); अर्थ (economic gain); काम (enjoyments of the pleasures of life); and मोक्ष (freedom from सṁसार). Of these, the mumukṣu should know that the real puruṣārtha is मोक्ष.
Upāya, or the means of लिबेरतिओन्, is five-fold: कर्म, ज्ञान, भक्ति, प्रपत्ति, and ācāryābhimāna. कर्म includes all such acts like यज्ञ, दान, सन्ध्या, पञ्चयज्ञस्, ध्यान, तीर्थयात्रा, etc. ज्ञान or ज्ञानयोग consists of self-renouncement (vairāgya) and ceaseless practice of contemplation on Lord नारायण. This leads to the realization of the Self, but not that of the Lord.
The next step is भक्ति. भक्ति or भक्तियोग marks the consummation of moral and spiritual endeavour as attained in the other two yogas. The Viśiṣṭādvaita constructs a ladder, as it were, from एथिच्स् to religion and from religion to mystic union. The seven aids to भक्ति are: विवेक (purification of the body as the living temple of God); vimoka (inner detachment); अभ्यास (ceaseless practice of the self-presence of God as the inner Self); kriyā (service to all beings); kalyāṇa (practice of virtues); anavasāda (freedom from despair); and anuddharṣa (absence of exultation).
Prapatti is complete self-surrender, and is meant for those who are unable to follow either कर्मयोग, ज्ञानयोग, or भक्तियोग. Its main characteristics are: to conceive what is in conformity with the will of God; to reject what is disagreeable to him; to seek him alone as the protector; and to surrender one’s self to him in all meekness.
Ācāryābhimāna is strong faith in the गुरु and his affectionate attachment to the disciple.
The obstacles to the spiritual path (virodhi), which are the last of the arthapañcaka, are again five-fold: obstacle to the realization of the Self, to the realization of God, to मोक्ष, to the means of realization, and to the attainment of the goal.
State of Liberation
The liberated सोउल् has a direct vision of ब्रह्मन् in वैकुण्ठ and is absorbed in the eternal bliss of union with him (sāyujya). To him the pluralistic world remains, but the pluralistic view is abolished. The distinction between him and ब्रह्मन् still remains, and there is no loss of personality. He will continue forever to enjoy this state of bliss by serving ब्रह्मन्.
Conclusion
Viśiṣṭādvaita is thus not a dry metaphysics, but a philosophy of religion. In it, reason and faith have been nicely synthesized. It guarantees the vision of God and salvation to all finite beings—human, subhuman, or celestial. The view that God is immanent in all for the purpose of cosmic redemption inspires the feeling that the God of all religions is ultimately one, though the various seers and sects may give different accounts of him.

Viśvakarma
(‘maker of every object’)
------------------------------------------
Viśvakarma was the famous architect, engineer and sculptor of the gods. As his very name suggests, he was the maker of practically every imaginable product.
He was the son of प्रभास (one of the eight वसुस्) and Yogasiddhi.
When he had completed his गुरुकुल-vāsa (living in the होउसे of the गुरु for एदुचतिओन्) his गुरु and his family made some impossible demands as गुरुदक्षिणा (fees) such as an eternally new होउसे, indestructible cloths and so on. He performed तपस्, pleased शिव and got divine power by which he became an expert in all fields of arts and crafts.
He is said to have shaped the सुदर्शन disc of विष्णु out of a part of सूर्य’s (Sun-god) orb.

Viṣṇu
------------------------------------------
Viṣṇu, also known as Mahāviṣṇu, is the second deity of the Hindu Trinity. He represents Sattvaguṇa and is the centripetal force as it were, responsible for sustenance, protection and maintenance of the created universe.
Etymologically speaking, the word ‘Viṣṇu’ means ‘one who pervades, one who has entered into everything.’ So he is the transcendent as well the immanent reality of the universe. He is the inner cause and power by which things exist.
Another name of विष्णु which is extremely common and popular is नारायण. The word means:
One who has made the causal waters his abode;
One who is the abode of all human beings;
One who has made the hearts of human beings his abode;
One who is the final goal of all human beings.
The first interpretation has given rise to a description of नारायण which is common and popular, as follows:
After the destruction of the universe of the previous cycle and before the च्रेअतिओन् of the next, नारायण, the Supreme God, falls asleep on his bed of the great serpent शेष (also called अनन्त), which is floating on the waters of the ocean क्षीरसमुद्र (‘ocean of milk’). One of his legs is resting on the lap of his consort लक्ष्मी, who is gently pressing it. When he is dreaming as it were, of the next च्रेअतिओन्, a lotus springs forth from his navel along with god ब्रह्मा seated on it. After waking up, he instructs ब्रह्मा to proceed with the act of च्रेअतिओन्.
This is a highly allegorical picture. The ocean represents causal waters from which all life springs, a concept not uncommonly found in other religions also. Or, since it is क्षीरसमुद्र, the ocean of milk, it stands for the purest form of प्रकृति or nature in its undifferentiated state, whiteness indicating this purity.
Out of the several equivalents of the word āpas (= water), is the word अमृत (= nectar, signifying bliss also). Hence we can say that the Lord नारायण is floating on the ocean of bliss, which is as it should be.
The serpent शेष or अनन्त is said to have a thousand heads and is supporting the worlds on its hoods. अनन्त, which literally means the ‘endless’ or ‘infinite’ actually stands for cosmic time which is infinite or endless. Created worlds come into being in time and are sustained in time. This is the meaning of the thousand hoods supporting the worlds. The thousand hoods simply indicate the innumerable divisions of time.
The concept of the thousand hoods supporting the worlds can also lead to the interpretation that the serpent represents the cosmic space, in which everything exists.
The word Śeśa is also significant. It actually means ‘the remainder,’ ‘what is leftover at the end’. Since च्रेअतिओन् cannot proceed out of nothing, it is to be assumed that ‘something’ is ‘leftover’ (śeṣa) from the previous च्रेअतिओन्, which forms the seed as it were, for the next. So, शेष represents the totality of the jīvas or indi-vidual souls in their subtle form, leftover from the previous cycle and needing more opportunities for regeneration.
Serpent can also represent काम or desire which is always leftover (śeṣa), even after acquisition and enjoyment of the desired object. This goes on until मोक्ष or final लिबेरतिओन्. Hence, in a cosmic sense, it can stand for the desire of the Lord to proceed with the next cycle of च्रेअतिओन् after rest!
Viṣṇu is always described as Nīlameghaśyāma, of a dark blue hue like that of the rain-bearing cloud. Since the infinite empty space appears as deep blue in colour, it is but proper that विष्णु the all-pervading cosmic power, be depicted as blue in colour.
The commonest form of the विष्णु icon has one face, four arms holding शङ्ख (conch), चक्र (discus), गदा (mace), पद्म (lotus) and he wears a necklace with the famous gem कौस्तुभ dangling on the lock of hair known as Śrīvatsa, on the left chest. He is also wearing a garland (of gems, or fragrant flowers) वैजयन्ती by name.
The four arms represent the four quarters, hence, absolute power of the Lord in all directions. The शङ्ख represents the five elements like the earth, water etc. चक्र stands for the चोस्मिच् मिन्द्. गदा indicates the cosmic intellect and the पद्म points to the evolving world. Just as the lotus is born out of water and unfolds gradually in all its glory, this world also is born out of the causal waters and evolves gradually in all its splendour. Hence the lotus stands for the evolved world. This world can be created only by a combination of the five elements, the मिन्द्, and the intellect. Hence the total meaning of this symbology would be that the Lord विष्णु is the creator and master of this world. The curl of hair, Śrīvatsa, represents all objects of enjoyment, the products of nature. The gem कौस्तुभ, resting on it, stands for the enjoyer. So, this world of duality, consisting of the enjoyer and the enjoyed, is like an ornament for the Lord. The garland वैजयन्ती is symbolical of the subtle elements (bhūta-तन्मात्रस्).
Sometimes two more weapons, नन्दक the sword (representing wisdom) and शार्ङ्ग the bow (representing the cosmic senses) are added to the arsenal of Lord विष्णु.
AVATĀRAS (INCARNATIONS) OF LORD VIṢṆU
To ward off the extraordinary perils to which mankind is prone—maybe the visitations from the demons, maybe from the human malefactors—and to preserve the socio-ethical order, Lord विष्णु whose duty it is to preserve this world, often incarnates himself. Though such incarnations are popularly considered to be ten, there is no limit to their number. Nor are there any restrictions regarding the time and place of their appearance. Whenever धर्म declines and अधर्म prospers he bodies himself forth to restore the balance in the world.
In the मत्स्यावतार (Fish-इन्चर्नतिओन्), the Lord is said to have saved मनु (the progenitor of mankind) and the सप्तर्षिस् (the seven sages, मिन्द्-born sons of ब्रह्मा) along with their wives during the deluge. The world was repopulated through them later on.
Lord विष्णु incarnated himself as the कूर्म (the Tortoise) in order to support the mount मन्दर which started sinking during the churning of the ocean (Samudramathana). The gods and the demons had jointly undertaken this adventure to get अमृत (nectar) from the ocean.
Next in the series is the Varāhāva-tāra (Boar-इन्चर्नतिओन्) in which the Lord killed the demon हिरण्याक्ष and lifted the earth out of the flood waters in which it had been submerged. This may be a symbolic representation of the extrication of the world from the deluge of sin by the power of the Supreme Being.
When प्रह्लाद, the great devotee of विष्णु was being severely tortured by his ड़थेर्, the demon हिरण्यकशिपु (who was a non-believer in the existence of an omnipresent and omnipotent God), नरसिṁह (Man-lion) appeared, emerging out of the pillar shown by him and killed him. Being a combination of man (the best of higher creatures) and lion (the best of lower creatures) नरसिṁह represents the best of च्रेअतिओन्. Incidentally this also proves the omnipresence of God. नरसिṁह is especially the embodiment of valour which is a divine attribute and is hence worshipped by rulers and warriors. His मन्त्र is said to be very powerful, capable of destroying enemies and exorcising evil.
When बलि the grandson of प्रह्लाद conquered the three worlds, इन्द्र was deprived of his heavenly kingdom. At the request of अदिति, the मोथेर् of इन्द्र, Lord विष्णु incarnated as वामन (the dwarf), a young ब्राह्मण boy, and approached बलि who was known for his munificence, for a gift of land that could be covered by three steps. With the first and the second he covered the earth and हेअवेन् and with the third, he pushed down बलि to the netherworld. Hence he is also known as त्रिविक्रम, one who encompassed the world with three big steps.
This myth teaches us that since even God had to resort to the dwarf’s form while begging, one who begs makes himself small! Secondly, a true ब्राह्मण can conquer the three worlds by the power of the spirit.
These five avatāras have been referred to in the various sections of the वेदस्.
The next five incarnations are in the human form.
Paraśurāma (Rāma with the battle-axe) is the sixth अवतार. Born as the son of the sage-couple, जमदग्नि and रेणुका, he exterminated the tyrannical among the kṣattriyas led by Kārtavīrya, who were oppressing the people. Whether this story has any historical basis and represents the struggle for supremacy between the ब्राह्मणस् and kṣattriyas, it is difficult to say.
Śrī राम, the next इन्चर्नतिओन्, meets परशुराम and absorbs his power into himself. Hence परशुराम is sometimes considered आवेशावतार, an इन्चर्नतिओन् by the temporary possession of विष्णु’s powers.
Śrī राम, one of the two most popular incarnations of the Lord विष्णु, comes next in the series. His story is too well-known to need any repetition. He typifies the ideal man. His story, the Rāmāyaṇa has now become an immortal epic. His name is known as the ‘Tāraka-मन्त्र,’ the मन्त्र that takes one across the ocean of transmigration.
Balarāma, ‘Rāma the strong,’ the elder brother of Śrī कृष्ण, is the eighth इन्चर्नतिओन्. His many adventures include the slaying of the ape Dvivida and the demon Dhenuka, shaking the ramparts of Hastināvati (the capital city of the Kauravas) and dragging the river यमुना out of its course. The story that the serpent शेष issued forth from his mouth at the time of his death gives credence to the belief that he was the इन्चर्नतिओन् of शेष. Some scholars basing their conjecture on the weapon of बलराम (the hala or plough), opine that he was an agricultural hero raised to the status of an अवतार in course of time.
Śrī कृष्ण, the ninth इन्चर्नतिओन् of Lord विष्णु is, perhaps, the most popular, so much so, that he is considered पूर्णावतार (the इन्चर्नतिओन् in toto) and all other deities are regarded as his manifestations. His story and his exploits are too numerous and too well-known to be mentioned here. To the average Hindu, he is the supreme statesman, warrior, hero, philosopher and teacher, nay, God Himself. He is the great expounder of the ‘Song Celestial,’ the Bhagavadgītā.
The tenth अवतार कल्कि, is yet to come. He will descend upon the earth at the end of the present age (Kali Yuga). Riding on the back of a white horse, with a drawn sword, he will destroy the enemies of धर्म and re-establish it in all its glory.
This list of the ten avatāras of Lord विष्णु is by no means the standard one accepted by all. Taking Śrī कृष्ण as विष्णु himself, he is not included in some lists. His place is taken over by बुद्ध. In some other lists, बुद्ध replaces बलराम. Iconographically speaking, बुद्ध seems to have disappeared from such lists only after the 15th century.
Strangely enough, the purpose of the बुद्ध-इन्चर्नतिओन् was supposed to be to mislead men of low birth and genius, who had become too proficient in the sacred lore and were a threat to the supremacy of the gods! This looks more like a joke than a serious proposition. It is obvious that the Hindus sealed the fate of बुद्धिस्म् in this country by absorbing बुद्ध into the pantheon of the avatāras.
Haṁsa, सात्वत, यज्ञ, दत्तात्रेय and वेदव्यास are some of the avatāras included in other lists, keeping the total as ten only. The number, however, rises sometimes to as high as twenty-three.
CATURVYŪHAS
The भागवत or the Pāñcarātra religion, which preaches the cult of विष्णु-नारायण, puts forth the theory that the Supreme Lord विष्णु has four aspects of manifestation:
the पर or the supreme;
the Vyūha or the emanation;
the विभव or the इन्चर्नतिओन् and
the Arca or icon.
Para is the Supreme as He is, in all His glory. विभव represents the incarnations already dealt with. Arca is the descent of the Lord into the icon ceremonially installed and worshipped in the temples.
The व्यूहस् or the emanations are four in number. Hence the term चतुर्व्यूहस्, also called चतुर्मूर्तिस्. They are: वासुदेव, सङ्कर्षण, प्रद्युम्न and अनिरुद्ध. According to Vaiṣṇava mythologies, while Śrī कृष्ण is वासुदेव, his brother बलराम is सङ्कर्षण. प्रद्युम्न and अनिरुद्ध are कृष्ण’s son and grandson respectively. Historically speaking, it is possible that these Yādava heroes were, in course of time, apotheosised into these व्यूहस्. Symbo-logically, वासुदेव represents चित्त (mind-stuff), whereas सङ्कर्षण stands for अहङ्कार (egoity), प्रद्युम्न for बुद्धि (intellect) and अनिरुद्ध for मनस् (mind). They represent the cosmic psychological evolution.
Later on, these व्यूहस् were increased to as many as twenty-four. Iconographically, all these व्यूहस् are identical in appearance except for the arrangement of the four emblems—śaṅkha, चक्र, गदा and पद्म.
The Pāñcarātra theology often adds another aspect of the manifestations, viz., the अन्तर्यामिन् (the indweller), which obviously cannot be represented through icons.
MINOR INCARNATIONS
Hindu म्य्थोलोग्य् abounds in stories of Lord विष्णु’s avatāras, which may be pūrṇāvatāras (full manifestations) like Śrī कृष्ण, aṁśāvatāras (partial manifestations) like कपिल or āveśāvarāras (temporary infilling of the divine power) like परशुराम. A few of these may now be dealt with.
Dattātreya
He was the son of the great sage अत्रि and his wife अनसूया, one of the paragons of chastity in Hindu म्य्थोलोग्य्. He was the originator of certain magical rites and the creator of the सोम plant. He was a teacher of non-Āryan people. Association with people of low birth and objects of pleasure has made him ritually impure. But, learning and enlightenment have made him so pure that nothing can ever stain him. Being the इन्चर्नतिओन् of the Trinity, he is shown as having three heads, six hands and accompanied by four dogs of different colours which represent the four वेदस्.
The दत्तात्रेय concept may be an attempt at harmonising the three cults of ब्रह्मा, विष्णु and शिव. It may also have been the medium through which non-Vedic cults were brought into the Hindu fold.
Dhanvantari
Dhanvantari rose from the ocean, at the time of churning, holding the अमृत-कलश (pot of ambrosia) in his hand. He is the originator of medical sciences. Reborn as the king of काशी he brought medical science to the earth.
Vedas also mention a धन्वन्तरि, a god associated with herbs and medicines.
He is described as a handsome person holding the pot of ambrosia and seated in front of विष्णु’s insignias.
Hayagrīva or Hayaśīrṣa
Yājñavalkya, the great sage, lost the Yajurveda as a result of his गुरु’s curse and performed severe penance.
Sun-god, pleased by his penance, appeared before him as a deity with the horse’s head and taught him the same Veda in another form. This section has come to be known as the Vājasaneyī Saṁhitā (vāji = horse). The origins of the हयग्रीव अवतार (the deity with the horse’s head) are perhaps found here.
Two demons मधु and कैटभ had stolen the वेदस् and hidden them under water. Lord विष्णु took the form of हयग्रीव, dived to the bottom of the ocean and rescued them after killing the demons.
Hayagrīva is the god of learning, akin to the goddess सरस्वती.
He is shown in the human form, with the horse’s head, possessing four or eight arms, carrying the various weapons and emblems of विष्णु.
Kapila
Kapila, the son of कर्दम and Devahūtī was a great sage who reduced to ashes the sixty thousand sons of the king सगर, just by a glance. Probably this story is at the back of his being identified sometimes with अग्नि. He taught Sāṇkhya philosophy to his मोथेर्.
Kapila icons usually have the hair dressed up as a crown (jaṭā-मुकुट), a beard, four arms, two of which are in योग holding a pitcher and the other two holding शङ्ख and चक्र.
Mohinī
At the behest of the gods who had been deprived of the ambrosia by the demons during the churning of the ocean, Lord विष्णु appeared as मोहिनी, the enchantress, who successfully duped the demons and distributed the nectar among the gods. Even शिव is said to have been bewitched by her beauty.
The story teaches us that इम्मोर्तलित्य् (amṛtatva) can be gained only by the conquest of delusion (moha).
Mohinī is shown as a beautiful young woman wearing colourful garments, decorated with ornaments and carrying a vase of nectar in hand.
Nara-Nārāyaṇa
After the purpose of नरसिṁह-अवतार was accomplished, नरसिṁह split himself into two, the lion part becoming the sage नारायण and the human part the sage नर. नर and नारायण then retired to बदरिकाश्रम for performing austerities. When इन्द्र tried to seduce them through celestial nymphs, Nārayaṇa produced the nymph ऊर्वशी from his thigh (ūru = thigh) who was more beautiful than all of them put together.
According to another version, these sages were sons of धर्म and अहिṁसा. They performed severe austerities and successfully vanquished the demon Sahasrakavaca (one who has a thousand armours).
These sages were reborn later as Śrī कृष्ण and अर्जुन.
This story has an important lesson for us. Everyone of us is a mixture of the human and the divine elements. The anti-human and the anti-divine demon is ever attempting to seduce us with his thousand wiles. To successfully vanquish him, we need to perform तपस् or austerity.
Nara-नारायण is represented either as a single person or as two persons. In the former case the icon may have two or four arms carrying the जपमाला (rosary) or the usual emblems of Lord विष्णु. In the latter case, नर may be shown as having two heads and two arms and wearing the deer skin. नारायण is depicted with the usual four arms carrying the emblems शङ्ख, चक्र, पद्म and जपमाला.
Vyāsa
Vyāsa is a cosmic entity born in every age to propagate the scriptures.
The sage कृष्ण-द्वैपायन, the son of पराशर, is the well-known व्यास of this age. He got that name since he collected all the extant Vedic hymns and divided them (vyas = to divide) into the four वेदस्. He is the author of the great epic Mahābhārata as also all the पुराणस् (mythologies) and the Brahmasūtras.
In images, he is shown as of slender build, dark in complexion and with the hair dressed up as a crown. His four disciples पैल, वैशम्पायन, जैमिनि and सुमन्तु are also shown by his side.
Yajña
Viṣṇu has been identified with यज्ञ or sacrifice in early Vedic literature. The Bhāgavata calls वराहावतार as यज्ञ-varāha and identifies his limbs with the various parts of a sacrifice. In other mythological lore, he as Yajñeśa, is described as the son of Ruci and Ākūti. The entire universe which is in a constant state of flux is like a sacrifice and the Lord responsible for this च्रेअतिओन् is looked upon as the personification of that sacrifice. Hence he is यज्ञ or Yajñeśvara.
His image has two heads, seven hands, three legs and four horns. The hands carry the sacrificial implements like ājyapātra (vessel holding the ghee) sruk, sruva and जुहू (various kinds of spoons and ladles), apart from शङ्ख and चक्र.
Obviously this is a symbolical representation, the various limbs representing the various items of the sacrifice. The description is rather too technical to be dealt with in a small essay like this.
OTHER ASPECTS OF विष्णु COMMONLY WORSHIPPED
Jagannātha of Puri in Orissa is a Vaiṣṇava deity which draws huge crowds, especially during the annual car festival. The image appears rather grotesque and is shaped out of a log and has prominent eyes. Once in twelve years the log-image is renewed, the log being brought every time mysteriously. The insertion of some ancient relic into the new image sanctifies it. It represents Śrī कृष्ण, with similar images representing बलराम and सुभद्रा (Kṛṣṇa’s sister).
Pāṇḍuraṅga Viṭṭhala commonly known as Viṭṭhala or Viṭhoba is the deity of the famous विष्णु temple at Pandharpur in Maharashtra. In fact, the word ‘Viṭṭha’ is a corrupted form of the word विष्णु. Rakumābāi (Rukmiṇī) is his consort standing by his left side.
This is the form of the Lord विष्णु revealed to a ब्राह्मण, Puṇḍali by name, because of his intense devotion to his parents.
Raṅganātha, along with वरदराज of काञ्चीपुरम् and वेङ्कटेश of तिरुपति, is the most popular aspect of विष्णु worshipped in South India. The well-known temple at श्रीरङ्गम् in Tamil Nadu is the very heart of the श्रीवैष्णव cult. This temple—at least the original icon—is said to have been born out of the ocean and given by Śrī राम to विभीषण. While carrying it from अयोध्या to लङ्का, विभीषण placed it on the ground at the present site, in order to rest a while. Unfortunately for him (and fortunately for others!) it got firmly fixed there!
The image is of the Yogaśayana type (lying on the serpent-bed in योग) with only two hands, the right hand apparently supporting the head while the left rests on the serpent-bed.
The lotus with ब्रह्मा, the आयुध-puruṣas (the weapons in human form), the demons मधु and कैटभ who were killed by him, as also some sages like भृगु and मार्कण्डेय are often depicted along with the Lord.
Similar Yogaśayana images are found in Srirangapatna and Shivasamudram of Karnataka and Tiruvanantapuram of Kerala where it is known as Padmanābha or Anantaśayana.
Varadarāja, the king among the bestowers of boons, is another aspect of Lord विष्णु which is very popular. Also known as Karivarada, it represents that aspect of the Lord responsible for saving Gajendra, the elephant king, from the death-clutches of the crocodile.
He is shown as riding on his vehicle गरुड and in the act of discharging the discus. The elephant Gajendra with its foot caught by the powerful teeth of the crocodile is also shown. Sometimes a human figure with its hands in obeisance is also shown near the crocodile, to represent the Gandharva (a demigod) who had been delivered from his curse which had resulted in his birth as a crocodile.
The temple of वरदराज at Kāñcī-puram in South India is one of the most important and famous विष्णु temples.
Veṅkaṭeśa, also known as Veṅka-ṭeśvara, श्रीनिवास or बालाजी of तिरुपति in Andhra Pradesh is perhaps the most popular of all the Hindu deities in our country and the temple on the तिरुपति hills gets fabulous income. The word Veṅgaḍam of Tamil origin signifies a hill. So वेङ्कटेश is the Lord of the hill. The story goes that Lord विष्णु as Varāha (the Boar) decided to continue his stay on the earth and that गरुड brought down the hill of वैकुण्ठ to earth for the Lord’s residence. Lord श्रीनिवास or वेङ्कटेश, another aspect of विष्णु, also manifested himself there at that time to reside on the earth for the good of mankind.
The image is said to be an Udbhava-mūrti (spontaneously manifested) and does not conform to known Āgama traditions. As regards the exact nature and form of the image, doubts exist, some opining that it represents हरिहर, and others, considering it as सुब्रह्मण्य or even देवी.
Viṣvaksena or ‘the all-conquering’ is an aspect of विष्णु, which occupies the same place in Vaiṣṇava tradition as गणेश in the Śaiva tradition. He is worshipped at the beginning of any undertaking, to avoid obstacles. He is shown with four hands, wearing शङ्ख, चक्र and गदा in three hands and the fourth exhibiting the tarjanīmudrā (threatening finger pose). The right leg is usually hanging down from the pedestal.
Viṣvaksena is also depicted sometimes as the gate-keeper or chief attendant of Lord विष्णु. He is shown standing on a white lotus and with long matted hair as also a beard. He represents the worldly sciences.
MINOR DEITIES ASSOCIATED WITH VIṢṆU
Garutmān or गरुड, the mighty bird-vehicle of Lord विष्णु is a minor deity invariably found in all the Vaiṣṇava temples. He is described as the son of the sage couple कश्यप and विनता and as the younger brother of अरुण, the charioteer of Sun-god. The chief among his multifarious exploits is his bringing of the pot of nectar from इन्द्र’s हेअवेन्. It is precisely this that made Lord विष्णु choose him as his vehicle.
Literally, the word गरुड means ‘wings of speech’. He actually personifies Vedic knowledge. On his wings, as it were, Vedic knowledge has come down to us, from the world of God.
The गरुड image is usually anthropomorphic. He is shown with a sharp beak, and two wings at the back. The hands may be eight or four or just two. Two of the hands are always in the adoration pose. In the others, he carries the conch, wheel, mace, sword, snake and nectar pot. The image is usually installed right opposite the central shrine.
It may appear to be rather intriguing that Lord विष्णु has a serpent as his couch and an eagle, its arch enemy, as his vehicle! This is to show that he is the Lord of balance and harmony which is an essential quality for one charged with the responsibility of sustaining this multi-farious universe.
Another deity invariably found in the विष्णु temples, especially in the South, is हनुमान् the monkey-god. The Rāmāyaṇa pictures him as a highly erudite, cultured and refined person. He is as strong as he is wise, and as devoted as he is strong, a rare combination indeed.
He is represented in two postures: When in the company of Śrī राम, सीता and लक्ष्मण, he is shown standing humbly at a distance or sitting devotedly at the feet of Śrī राम. In shrines specially erected for him, he strikes a heroic pose, usually with the mace in his left hand and carrying the Sañjīvinī mountain in his right hand.
Apart from these, it is common to show the weapons of Lord विष्णु also in human form. They are then called आयुध-puruṣas (weapon-beings). The आयुध-पुरुष may be male, female, or neuter, depending upon the gender of the word indicating it. For instance, गदा (mace) is a female deity whereas the चक्र (discus) is a neuter deity.
The सुदर्शन-चक्र is shown as a person with a hexagon as his background, brilliant as fire and having four or eight or sixteen arms holding bow, arrow, trident, noose, goad and other weapons as also implements, apart from the usual Vaiṣṇavite symbols. It is said to represent the चोस्मिच् मिन्द्, the will of the Lord to multiply as well as his infinite power to create and destroy the universe. The सुदर्शन-मन्त्र is said to possess the power to neutralise poisons and exorcise malignant spirits.
The कौमोदकी, the गदा (mace) of Lord विष्णु is depicted as a female deity, with one face and two hands which are in the posture of adoration. It symbolises power and sovereignty.
No account of Lord विष्णु will be complete without mentioning the Śāla-grāma (See ŚĀLAGRĀMA.), a blackish rounded and polished stone with a hole containing the fossils of tiny molluscs, which is worshipped as an emblem of His. There are several varieties of them representing different aspects of the Lord. Śālagrāmas can be installed in temples but are usually worshipped in one’s own home privately. Once it is kept at home, its worship becomes obligatory.

viṣṇubali
(‘offering to विष्णु’)
------------------------------------------
This is a rite performed by the husband of a pregnant lady during the eighth month. It should be done on the 2nd, 7th or the 12th day of the bright fortnight when the मोओन् is in the स्तर्स् Śrāvaṇa, रोहिणी or पुष्य.
Its purpose is to remove all harm to the foetus and assure an easy and safe delivery. It should be performed during every conception.
Nāndīśrāddha is to be done on the previous day. The next day, a होम has to be performed to विष्णु with 64 oblations of boiled rice mixed with ghee using Ṛgvedic mantras (such as 1.22.16-21; 10.90.1-16 and so on).
To the northeast of the fire a square plot with 64 small squares should be prepared. Cooked rice balls are kept in these squares. They are offered first by the Ṛgvedic mantras. One ball from them is offered to विष्णु with the मन्त्र Oṁ namo nārāyaṇāya. The husband and wife should partake of two rice balls of the same separately as prasāda or consecrated ड़ोओद्.

Viśvanātha Temple
------------------------------------------
Kāśī or वाराणसी (in the State of Uttar Pradesh) is the most ancient city of the world. Its presiding deity is Viśvanātha (‘Lord of the universe’) in the form of a लिङ्ग. This is one of the twelve ज्योतिर्लिङ्गस् (‘liṅgas of light’), manifestation of God in the form of a pillar of fire, as mentioned in the पुराणस्.
The ancient temple of Viśvanātha has been demolished several times by the Muslim fanatics and rebuilt by the devout Hindus. The present temple is the one built by Ahalyābāi Hoḷkar, the queen of Indore, in A.

. There is reason to believe that the original लिङ्ग which had been thrown into the Jñānavāpī or Gyānvāpī well (‘well of enlightenment’) nearby, was surreptitiously recovered, quietly preserved and later installed in this temple. It was ceremonially reconsecrated.
The temple is a stone structure situated in a quadrangle covered with a roof. Two towers and a dome (in between them) rise above the roof. The first tower is above the Daṇḍapāṇīśvara shrine and the second, over the sanctum of Viśva-nātha. On the last is a pole bearing a flag and a trident.
The temple has been built on a piece of land which is 9 metres (30 feet) square. The sanctum is about 2.6 metres (8.5 feet) square. The total height of the tower from the ground is 15 metres (51 feet).
There are beautiful carvings of different designs.
The temple is kept open from 3 A. M. to 11 P. M. Five āratis (ceremonial waving of light etc.) are done during this period.
Three days are considered extremely sacred in this temple for special decoration to the Lord Viśvanātha. They are: Kārttikaśukla-pratipad (first day of bright fortnight of Kārttika, in October/ November); Mahāśivarātri (Māgha-कृष्ण-caturdaśī, in February/March); Phālguna-śukla-एकादशी (in February/March).
Even today, the temple is extremely popular and is daily visited by thousands of devotees throughout the year.
See also KĀŚĪ.

Viṣṇusahasranāma
(‘thousand names of विष्णु)
------------------------------------------
In हिन्दुइस्म्, stotras or hymns of God are legion. Out of these, the aṣṭottara-śatanāmas (with 108 names) and sahasra-nāmas (with 1000 names) are a class by themselves.
In the latter group, two sahasra-nāmas are considered outstanding and extremely popular even now. They are: the Lalitāsahasranāma and the Viṣṇu-sahasranāma, dedicated respectively to the Divine मोथेर् ललिता (an aspect of देवी पार्वती) and Lord विष्णु or नारायण. In fact, they are considered, not as just hymns of praise, but as mantras (mystical texts) potent with spiritual vibrations.
The Viṣṇusahasranāma, like the Bhagavadgītā, is an integral part of the Mahābhārata (Anuśāsanaparva 149.1-142).
Verses 1 to 13 form the introduction called pūrvapīṭhikā. The actual Sahasra-nāma is spread over verses 14 to 120. Thereafter, the phalaśruti (fruits of recitation) is given in the last part comprising verses 121 to 142.
The recitation of such hymns as this is considered superior to the performance of वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् and is as good as a ritualistic worship of God due to the following reasons: It does not need the help of other human beings or money and materials. The rules of deśa (place of performance) and kāla (auspicious times) do not apply to its chanting. Irrespective of caste or creed all are free to chant it provided they have faith. It does not involve violence to living beings.
The deeper meaning and significance of such esoteric texts can be known only through the commentaries written by competent scholars. It is interesting to note that so far, at least 15 commentaries (in Sanskrit) have been discovered on this hymn. Out of these the following three are more well-known:
Śāṅkarabhāṣya by Śaṅkarācārya (A.

-812).
This has two subcommentaries:
Vivṛti by Tāraka-brahmānanda-सरस्वती; Padyaprasūnāñjali by Kavipaṇḍita Gambhirabhāratī.
Bhagavadguṇadarpaṇa by पराशर भट्ट (A.

-1206).
Satyasandhīya by Satyasandhatīrtha of Uttarādimaṭha (18th century).
These three commentaries represent the three main systems of Vedānta viz., Advaita, Viṣiṣṭādvaita and द्वैत.
The Viṣṇusahasranāma is mainly meant for chanting, either independently or as a part of a rite. The individual names may also be separately used in arcana (offering with flowers in worship).
For chanting it, there is a standard ritual method. First the names of the ṛṣi (the sage through whom it was revealed), the devatā (the deity to whom it is addressed) and the छन्दस् (the metre in which it is composed) have to be recited. For this hymn, these are: वेदव्यास, नारायण and anuṣṭubh.
This is followed by viniyoga or the purpose for which the hymn is chanted. Here, the general purpose is to please the Lord. However, if the devotee has any particular purpose or desire to be fulfilled, that may be properly mentioned.
Then comes ध्यान or meditation on the form of the deity. This is usually done by chanting a dhyānaśloka (hymn of meditation) which gives a detailed description of the form.
In the विष्णुसहस्रनाम tradition however, nine ślokas are given as ध्यान-ślokas and hence all of them are to be chanted.
As regards the actual chanting, two methods are being followed. In the first, the following is the sequence: ṛṣyādinyāsa; ध्यान; actual Sahasranāma (verses 14 to 120).
In the second, the introductory part (verses 1 to 13) and the phalaśruti (eulogy, verses 121 to 142) are also included. Sometimes, 8 more verses are added in the very beginning. Printed texts meant exclusively for chanting contain all these details.
Bhīṣma the grandsire was laying down on the bed of arrows, awaiting death at an auspicious moment. It was during this period that he was teaching the duties of a king to युधिष्ठिर the eldest of the Pāṇḍavas. The Viṣṇusahasranāma was taught by him then, when युधिष्ठिर put him six questions about the highest God who has to be praised and worshipped, and repetition of whose name will lead to लिबेरतिओन्.
There are exactly 1000 names in the hymn. Though some of the names have been repeated more than once, the commentators have justified them with appropriate explanations.
From out of these thousand names, Hindu religious tradition has selected a few, to be used in an appropriate form, to fulfil one’s desires. For instance:
Mantra for जप, Desired Fruit
Oṁ kāmapradāya namaḥ (298), Fulfilment of desires.
Om anantajite namaḥ (307), Victory in undertakings.
Oṁ sthānadāya namaḥ (387), Attainment of position and status in life.
Oṁ sthaviṣṭhāya namaḥ (436), Destruction of sins.
Oṁ samīhanāya namaḥ (444), Getting a good job.
Oṁ ratnagarbhāya namaḥ (473), Gaining wealth.
Oṁ praṇavāya namaḥ (957), Attaining लिबेरतिओन्.
The numbers in the brackets indicate the serial number of the name (according to the Śāṅkarabhāṣya).
The actual method of जप has to be learnt from the experts in the field of sādhana or spiritual practice.
One of the lists available gives 118 such mantras.
This much can definitely be said that the Viṣṇusahasranāma is extremely popular even now. It is extensively used in temple rituals and on religious occasions.

Viṣuvasaṅkrānti
------------------------------------------
Saṅkrānti is the apparent passage of the sun from one राशि (zodiacal sign) to the next following one. For instance, when the sun leaves धनुस् and enters मकर, it is designated Makarasaṅkrānti.
Meṣasaṅkrānti and Tulāsaṅkrānti are called विषुवसङ्क्रान्ति. On these tithis, the duration of day and night are equal.

Viṣṇudharmapurāṇa
------------------------------------------
This is an upapurāṇa which has not yet been printed. It is a fairly voluminous work dealing mainly with Vaiṣṇava philosophy and rituals. It might have been compiled during the third century A. D. It has 105 chapters and 4000 verses.
The work deals mainly with the rites and duties of the Vaiṣṇavas. Other subjects are: political administration, duties of women and a few legends.
Quite a few writers of स्मृति have drawn upon this work.

viśokā
(‘without sorrow’)
------------------------------------------
The मिन्द् is constantly rising in the form of vṛttis or waves of thoughts and emotions and hence difficult to control. पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.) in his monumental work the Yogasūtras, gives a few methods called parikarmas, in seven sūtras (1.33 to 39) which help in controlling the मिन्द्. One of them is indicated by this sūtra: viśokā vā jyotiṣmatī (1.36).
When the मिन्द् is directed towards the suṣumnānāḍī which is in the middle of the spinal column, but extends right up to sūryamanḍala (the orb of the sun), one is able to get a knowledge of one’s own चित्त or मिन्द्. This knowledge resembles light and results in freedom from sorrow (vi-śokā).

viṣṭi
------------------------------------------
This is a technical term used in Hindu अस्त्रोलोग्य्. (See PAÑCĀṄGA for details.)
Viṣṭi is half of a tithi (lunar day). The works on अस्त्रोलोग्य् have raised it to the status of an illformed malignant demoness. विष्टि has to be avoided for any auspicious undertaking. Works like the Bṛhatsaṁhitā prescribe a Viṣṭivrata to appease her.

Vishwa Hindu Parishad
------------------------------------------
The gradual deterioration of the Hindu society in its value system and unity, prompted a number of Hindu religious leaders to establish the विस्ह्wअ हिन्दु परिस्हद् in A.
. M. S. Golwalkar (A.

-1973) (the then Head of the well-known Rashtriya Swayam Sevak Sangh) played the key role in this venture.
Its headquarters is situated in New Delhi.
Its objectives are: Protection to and consolidation of the Hindu society; levelling up of the neglected sections of the society ultimately leading to greater integration and cohesion; bringing back all those who had left the Hindu fold and get them merged in the mainstream; establish contact with the Hindus living in foreign countries and help them to preserve Hindu values of life; actively spreading Hindu religion and culture.
Slowly and steadily it has expanded and become a world-wide organization. There are 40,000 committees spread over 11 regions of India. It has branches in 20 foreign countries.
The organizational wing includes: Youth-wing (called Bajrang Dal and दुर्गा Vahini); women’s wing; world co-ordination wing; research wing and full-time dedicated persons’ wing.
It has successfully undertaken several programmes in the religious, social and propaganda fields.
Vigorous attempts have been made to bring about unity among various maṭhas (monasteries and religious institutions), to train the arcakas (priests) of temples, to organize religious festivals in a proper manner, to spreading हिन्दुइस्म् through discourses, journals and publications and through social service activities.
The organization has successfully conducted several conventions of Hindu religious leaders during the period A.

-2007, to forge unity among them. General conventions called Hindu Sammelans have also been organized including those in foreign countries.
Protection of the cow and reconversion of the Hindus who had left the Hindu fold, have been important items of policy of the Vishwa Hindu movement.
There is no doubt that the organization is steadily gaining ground and becoming popular.

Viśvarūpa
(‘Cosmic Form’)
------------------------------------------
In the Bhagavadgītā (Chapter 11), at the specific request of अर्जुन, Lord कृष्ण shows him his विश्वरूप or the Cosmic Form, after endowing him with divine sight, since he could not see it with his ordinary sight.
The verses 10 to 31 describe this विश्वरूप.
The Lord in this Cosmic Form had innumerable heads and hands, decorated gorgeously and holding a large variety of weapons. He was blazing like a thousand suns. अर्जुन saw all beings in him—including ब्रह्मा the creator, the ṛṣis, right up to animals—stationed in a small part of his body. The Lord had pervaded all the worlds and appeared to be of infinite proportions. All the warriors on the battle field had entered into his mouths and were being mercilessly crushed.
Struck with great fear, अर्जुन prays to Him fervently, requesting Him to withdraw it and appear in his old, human, form.
Earlier, in the court of the Kauravas, when दुर्योधन spurns all proposals of peace put forward by Śrī कृष्ण to avoid war and behaves most arrogantly, even threatening to imprison him, Śrī कृष्ण exhibits his विश्वरूप (vide Mahābhārata, Udoyagaparva, Chapter 131).
Viśvarūpa (circa A.
) is the name of a commentator of Yājñavalkya Smṛti, the commentary itself being called Bālakrīḍā. Some scholars identify him with Sureśvarācārya, a direct disciple of शङ्कर (A.

Viṣṇusūkta
(‘the hymn [dealing with] विष्णु’)
------------------------------------------
The वेदस् contain several hymns known as Sūktas, addressed to different deities. The Ṛgveda itself is said to contain 1017 such Sūktas.
The Viṣṇusūkta is one such important hymn addressed to Lord विष्णु.
There are two versions, one being in the Ṛgveda and the other in the Taittirīya Saṁhitā. The former is actually a hymn of 45 ṛks or verses culled from four different places of the Ṛgveda. The latter is a smaller one with only 12 verses out of which eleven are taken from the Ṛgveda itself.
These sūktas may be ceremonially chanted as जप to get specific results or may be used in वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् at the appropriate places. For instance, if the मन्त्र ‘tad viprāso....’ (eleventh मन्त्र; also Ṛgveda 1.22.21) is repeated 100 times every day, the person who does it will remember Lord विष्णु at the time of death.
A brief summary of the twelve mantras (from the Taittirīya Saṁitā) may now be given: I praise the heroic deeds of विष्णु. It is he who has created all the worlds and their supervisory deities. He has traversed and measured all the worlds. He has established the सत्यलोक as the highest world for the benefit of the seekers.
(The next part of this मन्त्र is used to tie the festoon of grass to the shed housing the carts containing the सोम juice.)
The sky dear to him is allpervading. Those who want to reach him are performing sacrifices and giving gifts. In his world bliss is constantly flowing.
That विष्णु by whose power all the worlds are supported, is praised for transcending them through his three steps. He is being praised as the supreme even as the lion in a mountain is, by other animals.
O Lord विष्णु! None is able to know the limits of your cosmic body! We know only its two aspects—the earth and the sky. Other aspects like the heavenly worlds are known only to you.
This Lord विष्णु pervaded this earth in order to give it to the gods who requested him for it. Those who pray to him live a steady and happy life. It is he who has created these worlds to grant them to his votaries.
May that विष्णु who occupied the three worlds be our Master. His very name विष्णु shows his greatness.
May the gods protect us, who are living in that part of the earth, occupied by the cosmic strides of विष्णु!
When विष्णु occupied this earth through his three steps, it was covered over by the dust raised.
When विष्णु, the all-powerful protector traversed the worlds with his three cosmic steps, he automatically upheld all aspects of धर्म. Look at this विष्णु, the friend of इन्द्र, by whose grace one is able to perform the Vedic rites!
Just as one can perceive the all-pervading sky without any obstruction, the persons endowed with spiritual wisdom can see the highest Abode of विष्णु always.
The wise men highly praise this Abode of विष्णु with appropriate hymns.
(The last मन्त्र is a phalaśruti or eulogy. Its recitation results in correcting all the defects and confers victory on the person who recites.)
Most of these mantras are ṛks taken from the Ṛgveda. The commentators have also given the viniyoga (their use in वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस्) for them. For instance, the fifth मन्त्र (‘vicakrame pṛthivīmeṣa....’) is to be chanted in the sacrifice called Ukthya. The seventh मन्त्र (‘ato devā....’) has to be used in the दर्शपूर्णमास sacrifice during the oblations for the expiation of sins.

Viśvedevas
------------------------------------------
These are Vedic gods. Literally the word means ‘all the gods’. Perhaps, all the gods leftover without being specifically mentioned in prayers, are meant to be included under this word. But they gradually seem to evolve as a specific group like the Ādityas or the Maruts. These deities are the protectors of ṛta, the moral law. They destroy the enemies of their devotees, protect the good, give auspicious abodes, and control—like kings. They are ever young and handsome. They are easily pleased by devoted obeisance.
Later म्य्थोलोग्य् describes them usually as ten in number: Vasu (dwelling place), सत्य (truth), Kratu (will), दक्ष (skill), Kāla (time), काम (desire), Dhṛti (forbearance), कुरु (the ancestor of the Kurus), पुरूरवस् (a being dwelling in the atmosphere), Mādravas (cry of joy). These deities are said to be fond of funeral offerings.

Viṣṇutattvavinirṇaya
------------------------------------------
Madhvācārya (A.

-1317), the chief architect of द्वैत Vedānta, has 37 works to his credit. Out of them ten are prakaraṇagranthas or treatises dealing solely with his द्वैत philosophy. The Viṣṇutattvavinirṇaya is the most complete and outstanding among them.
It is in prose and is spread over three paricchedas or chapters. The first is the biggest and most exhaustive. The other two are very short.
God the Supreme, called विष्णु, नारायण, Hari or वासुदेव, can be known only through the sadāgamas or true scriptures. They are the वेदस्, the two epics and the Pāñcarātra texts. The वेदस् are the supreme authority since they are apauruṣeya (not a च्रेअतिओन् of human beings).
Viṣṇu is the Supreme Reality. मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन् is attained only by his grace. His grace can be got only by the knowledge of his greatness and devotion to him.
The identity of the जीव (the individual सोउल्) and ईश्वर (God)—as the advaitins aver—can never be proved in any way. Vedic sentences like tat-tvam-asi have been shown that they teach only difference and not identity.
The second chapter shows the greatness of विष्णु and his consort लक्ष्मी as also the inferiority of all other deities like ब्रह्मा and शिव.
The third—the last—chapter is devoted to prove how विष्णु is perfect, beyond all limitations.
Out of the several commentaries, the Aṇusudhā by जयतीर्थ (A.
-1388) is the best. It has seven sub-commentaries.

Viṣṇudharmasūtra
------------------------------------------
This is one of the dharmaśāstra works in the form of sūtras.
The text as available in print at present, seems to be a mixture of an earlier old part and a later part grafted on to it. The earlier prose part in the form of sūtras probably belongs to the period 300 B. C. to A.
. The later part in poetry may be assigned to the period A.

-600.
It has 100 chapters, most of them being brief or even very short.
A brief synopsis of the contents may now be given:
The four varṇas and their dharmas; duties of kings; various offences and their punishments; mixed castes and their offsprings; death-rites and associated rules; on marriages including inter-marriages; duties of women; various सṁस्कारस्; sins and expiations; descriptions of various hells; śrāddhas; anatomy of the human body; hymns of praise to वासुदेव by Bhū (Earth) and Śrī (Lakṣmī).
The whole work professes to be a revelation by Lord विष्णु. However it seems to borrow the material from other (earlier) smṛtis like those of मनु and याज्ञवल्क्य.
There is a commentary called Vaijayantī by नन्दपण्डित (A.
) which has been published.

Viṣṇupurāṇa
------------------------------------------
For over two millennia, the purāṇas—the most popular scriptures of Hinduism—have proved to be a source, not only of knowledge and wisdom but also of spiritual solace. Of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas, the Viṣṇupurāṇa is, perhaps, the earliest compilation (assigned to the period 100 B. C.-A.

) and accords well with the five general characteristics of the पुराणस् like sarga (creation), pratisarga (inter-mediate च्रेअतिओन्) and so on (See PURĀṆAS.).
Though the Viṣṇupurāṇa is said to have contained 23,000 verses, the printed texts as available now have only 6400 verses spread over 126 chapters, arranged in the form of six aṁśas or Books.
Unlike the other पुराणस् where generally the सूत रोमहर्षण narrates the stories after being questioned by some sages, this purāṇa is narrated by the sage पराशर (father of व्यास and grandson of वसिष्ठ) to his disciple मैत्रेय.
Though most of the work is in poetry, it has elegant prose passages also. In fact, it has all the characteristics of a good literary classic.
It has three commentaries:
Ātmaprakāśa by Śrīdhara (15th century A. D.); Vaiṣṇavākūtacandrikā by Ratnagarbha; and, Viṣṇucittīya by an unknown author.
The contents of the six aṁśas may now be given briefly as follows:
First Aṁśa (22 chapters; 1412 verses)
The 24 cosmic principles and the च्रेअतिओन् of the world; च्रेअतिओन् of beings like the prajāpatis, पितृस् and देवस्; stories of ध्रुव and प्रह्लाद; greatness of विष्णु.
Second Aṁśa (16 chapters; 789 verses)
Geographical details of this earth and of the 14 worlds; नवग्रहस् or the nine प्लनेत्स्; some astronomical details of स्तर्स् and प्लनेत्स्; stories of जडभरत, Ṛbhu and Nidāgha.
Third Aṁśa (18 chapters; 830 verses)
Manvantaras, मनुस् and their sons; व्यास and division of the वेदस्; the four varṇas and the āśramas; on śrāddha (obsequial rites) in detail.
Fourth Aṁśa (24 chapters; 1353 verses)
Lineages of वैवस्वत मनु and इक्ष्वाकु; story of Śrī राम; descriptions of Somavaṁśa, Yaduvaṁśa and कुरु-vaṁśa (i.e., the kings of those lineages); kings of the future up to the kings of Magadha; kalidharma or the character-istics of the कलि-age.
Fifth Aṁśa (38 chapters; 1517 verses)
Story of कृष्ण in great detail; mutual destruction of the Yādavas; चोरोनतिओन् of Parikṣit; final journey of the Pāṇḍavas.
Sixth Aṁśa (8 chapters; 498 verses)
Interesting and long description of the behaviour of the people in the कलियुग; greatness of the कलियुग since worship and singing the glories of Lord कृष्ण are enough to attain लिबेरतिओन्; description of प्रलय or dissolution of the world; eulogy of this purāṇa.
The Viṣṇupurāṇa has some special features which may now be dealt with under appropriate headings:
Philosophy
The philosophy of the Viṣṇupurāṇa is practically the same as the Vedānta of the उपनिषद्स्.
God the Absolute, though called विष्णु here, is not just the विष्णु of the Trinity responsible for the sustenance of the created world. He is परब्रह्मन्, of the nature of ज्ञान (knowledge or चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्) and absolutely pure. The appearance of this world as an entity separate from him is only an इल्लुसिओन् (

).
Brahmā, विष्णु and महेश्वर of the Trinity are actually the three aspects of this परमात्मन् as associated with the three guṇas (rajas, सत्त्व and तमस्) (vide
and 66;

; 1.9.56).
The description of the process of च्रेअतिओन् is similar to that of the Sāṅkhya philosophy (
-70). However, in this purāṇa विष्णु is the original and absolute cause. The world evolves out of him—called विष्णु (

) or कृष्ण (4.12.4)—through his power called प्रधान or प्रकृति.
Even the infinite numbers of the jīvas (individual beings) are the reflections of the one विष्णु seen due to अविद्या or nescience.
The purāṇa accepts the कर्म (or actions) sanctioned by the scriptures and भक्ति or devotion to God (Viṣṇu) as the primary means of मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन्. निष्कामकर्म (selfless action) purifies the मिन्द्. विष्णु gets established in such a मिन्द्. ध्यान or meditation on the beautiful form of विष्णु along with the repetition of the dvādaśākṣarīmantra (mantra of twelve syllables viz., oṁ namo bhagavate vāsudevāya) will lead to ज्ञान and मोक्ष.
However, the role of भक्ति has been highlighted, through the story of प्रह्लाद.
Vaṁśāvalis or Lineages
Another speciality of this purāṇa is the long lists of kings and their lineage belonging to the famous Sūryavaṁśa (Solar race) and the चन्द्र or सोम vaṁśa (Lunar race).
It is interesting to note that both these races start from विष्णु Himself!
The prominent kings of the Sūryavaṁśa include the following ones: Vivasvān, मनु, इक्ष्वाकु, Māndhātā, हरिश्चन्द्र, भगीरथ, दशरथ, Śrī राम and Agnivarṇa. The last king, Maru by name, is said to be in योग, living even now in the village Kalāpa. He will restart the vaṁśa in the next कृतयुग!
Another branch of the Sūryavaṁśa started with Nimi (the son of इक्ष्वाकु) in which the Janakas such as Janakavaideha and Sīradhvaja जनक, were the prominent ones. They excelled in spiritual wisdom.
In the Somavaṁśa or the चन्द्र-vaṁśa, the following kings were famous: चन्द्र, बुध, Purūrava, नहुष, धन्वन्तरि, ययाति, यदु, दुष्यन्त, कुरु, जरासन्ध, Kauravas and Pāṇḍavas. Śrī कृष्ण belonged to the Yaduvaṁśa.
Mahāpadmananda was the last king of the race descended from जरासन्ध.
Like Maru of the Sūryavaṁśa, देवापि of the चन्द्रवṁश is said to be the last king still alive in योग in the same village Kalāpa. He will restart the race in future.
Description of Kaliyuga
Though the Viṣṇupurāṇa gives a long description of the कलियुग, the age wherein people become unrighteous and evil to the core (vide

-58), it also points out the three advantages that people have in that age. They are: People get the highest spiritual benefits just by singing the names and glories of God; women get all the merit of the good deeds by serving their husbands sincerely; शूद्रस् attain religious merit by performing their duties well.
The विष्णुपुराण and the Bhāgavata
The Bhāgavata seems to be an elabo-ration of the stories and ideas contained in the Viṣṇupurāṇa. Whereas the latter deals only with five avatāras or incarnations out of the well-known ten, the Bhāgavata deals in detail with all the ten and a few more. Though भक्ति or devotion finds an important place in the Viṣṇupurāṇa, in the Bhāgavata it is allpervading. However, it has to be conceded that the language of the latter is quite archaic and tough whereas that of the former is simple and elegant.
Literary Grace
The Viṣṇupurāṇa has certain special features. Its language, though simple and elegant, is also highly poetic. Descriptions of nature are not only beautiful but also contain excellent similes bearing on philosophical and ethical principles (vide 5.10.2-15). There are verses praising Bharatakhaṇḍa (India) as karmabhūmi (the land of good deeds) and that one is born here only out of religious merit (

, 24).
There are also verses pregnant with worldly wisdom which have been used as subhāṣitas (maxims) (vide 4.10.26, 27).
There is no doubt that the Viṣṇupurāṇa has been a beacon light for the well-known classic, the Bhāgavata.
See also BHĀGAVATA and PURĀṆAS.

Viṣṇubhāga
(‘portion assigned to विष्णु’)
------------------------------------------
See BRAHMABHĀGA and ŚIVALIṄGA.

Viśvāmitra
(‘friend of all’)
------------------------------------------
Viśvāmitra, along with वसिष्ठ, is one of the most well-known ṛṣis or sages that we come across, not only in the वेदस् but also in the epics and the पुराणस्. He is the ṛṣi for the entire third मण्डल of the Ṛgveda. However, only 501 ṛks are directly attributed to him, the rest being assigned to his descendants.
His prayer to the rivers Vipāṭ and शुतुद्री (the modern Beas and Sutlej rivers in the Punjab State) to make way for him so that he could cross over safely and escape from the robbers pursuing him is famous as the Nadīsūkta (Ṛgveda 3.33).
He has been mentioned as a great sage by several texts of Vedic literature (vide ऐतरेय Āraṇyaka
; Taittirīya Saṁhitā
.2; Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa 15.1; Pañcaviṁśa Brāhmaṇa 1

).
In the story of शुनश्शेफ (Ṛgveda 1.24) विश्वामित्र appears as the saviour of the young man who had been earmarked to be killed in a Vedic sacrifice. विश्वामित्र adopts him as a son.
As per the Nirukta (2.24) and the Pañcaviṁśa Brāhmaṇa (21.12.2), Viśvā-मित्र was a king.
According to the epics and the पुराणस्, he was the son of the king Gādhi of चन्द्रवṁश, known first as Viśvaratha. He had several wives and sons.
The Rāmāyaṇa (Bālakāṇḍa, Chapters 51 to 65) gives his story in detail. This contains some important incidents like creating a हेअवेन् for the king त्रिशङ्कु, his conflict with वसिष्ठ and his ultimately being raised to the status of a ब्रह्मर्षि.
He is one of the सप्तर्षिस् (the Seven Sages) for the present age.
His greatest contribution was revealing the Gāyatrīmantra for the good of humanity.

Viṣvaksena
(‘one [who is] surrounded on all sides by the army’)
------------------------------------------
In the well-known hymn, the Viṣṇu-sahasranāma, this word has been used as one of the names of विष्णु (name 125).
When विष्णु is in the battle-field, fighting with the senā or army of the असुरस् or demons, they are so terrified that they run helter-skelter (= viṣvak). Hence he is called ‘Viṣvaksena’.
In the Pāñcarātra literature of वैष्णविस्म्, विष्वक्सेन is described as the commander of the minor deities surrounding विष्णु and hence called “Gaṇapati”. He is the equivalent of गणपति or विनायक of शैविस्म्.
According to one version he was the son of वरुण and Suvarcalā. He pleased Lord विष्णु by severe austerities spread over twelve years. Gratified with his devotion, विष्णु made him the senāpati or the commander of his forces.
In the श्रीवैष्णव line of teachers, he occupies the third place, just after विष्णु and लक्ष्मी. His image is installed in all the विष्णु temples of this sect. He is said to be the custodian of the nirmālya or flowers used by the main deity विष्णु.
Iconographical works describe him as almost similar to विष्णु but without the śrīvatsa mark on the chest. He holds the शङ्ख (conch), चक्र (discus), and गदा (mace) in three hands, the fourth exhibiting the tarjanīmudrā (pose of threatening [the evil-doers]).
He may be shown as seated upon a throne. His consort is Jayā, also called वाराही.
